"The day they put it in and I turned it on, I was up seven flights of stairs before they stopped me. BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) — Timothy Connick endured six years of agony. At night, as he lay in bed, it felt as though a pair of scissors were lodged in his foot. “I turn over, and it’s just like they’re getting jammed in more.”

Connick found relief from chronic pain through a peripheral nerve stimulator implanted above his hip. Connick, 52, of Lynn, Massachusetts, injured his foot 11 years ago after falling from a loading dock at work. “I fell about seven feet onto the concrete and smashed my heel. It started hurting that moment and kept hurting for six years after that.”

Connick is one of millions. According to the American Chronic Pain Association, as many as one in three American adults suffer from chronic pain. The organization defines chronic pain as “pain that continues a month or more beyond the usual recovery period for an injury or illness or that goes on for months or years because of a chronic condition.” The group says the pain is usually not constant, but it can significantly disrupt a sufferer’s life.

Over the years, Connick consulted multiple doctors and tried two dozen medications for pain management, but nothing relieved the pain or the depression that followed. “It was pretty much a no-win situation as long as that pain was going to be there,” he recalls.

He was eventually referred to neurologist Anne Louise Oaklander, director of the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. “Pain is the No. 1 reason why patients seek medical care, but until recently it hasn’t been part of the medical school curriculum,” she says. “Many physicians and nurses feel uncomfortable and unqualified to treat these patients.”

Oaklander sees many patients whom she describes as “bouncing around the health care system” for years without a firm diagnosis. She divides chronic pain sufferers into two groups.

“One is the group that has an ongoing cause of their pain,” she says. “The classic example of that is patients with arthritis. They have pain in their joints every day.”

Far more difficult, she says, is the second group: “Patients who have chronic pain without an obvious cause of tissue injury.”

Connick falls into the second category, Oaklander says, noting that X-rays show broken bones but not nerve damage. “It was only many years later when he was examined by a neurologist that his underlying nerve injury was identified and able to be treated,” she said.

Oaklander says pain medications can help most patients, but other options are available. For example, she says, if the pain is related to an orthopedic problem, physical therapy may be the best choice.

In Connick’s case, relief came through surgery to implant a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip. Based on pacemaker technology, the stimulator is placed under the skin and works by emitting benign pulses that override pain signals to the brain, Oaklander explains. She cautions that minor surgery is involved and that the device works in only about half of the patients who receive it.

For Connick, it made all the difference. “The day they put it in and I turned it on, I was up seven flights of stairs before they stopped me. Everything that I hadn’t been able to do and everything that made me happy was back available to me again and I knew it right away.”

These days, Connick is back at work loading trucks. He is on his feet all day and does not complain of any pain.

Oaklander concludes: “If you have chronic pain, don’t take no for an answer. ... I think it’s important for chronic pain patients to keep a sense of purpose, optimism and hope despite the indignities that many are subjected to.”

BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) — For six years, Timothy Connick lived with severe pain. At night, when he lay in bed, he said it felt like scissors were protruding from his foot. “When I roll over, it feels like they’re being pushed in even deeper,” he said.

Connick, who found relief after doctors implanted a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip, is 52 and lives in Lynn, Massachusetts. His pain began 11 years earlier, after he was hurt on the job when he fell from a loading dock. “I dropped about seven feet onto concrete and crushed my heel,” he recalled. “It hurt immediately, and it kept hurting for the next six years.”

He is far from alone. The American Chronic Pain Association says up to one-third of adults in the United States experience chronic pain. The group describes chronic pain as pain that lasts at least a month beyond the normal healing time for an illness or injury, or pain that persists for months or years because of a long-term condition. The association notes that chronic pain is often not continuous, but it can seriously interfere with a person’s daily life.

Connick spent years seeing a number of doctors and trying roughly two dozen pain medications. None relieved either the physical pain or the depression that came with it. “As long as the pain was still there, it felt like there was no way to win,” he said.

Eventually, he was sent to Dr. Anne Louise Oaklander, a neurologist who directs the nerve injury unit at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. Oaklander said pain is the leading reason people seek medical treatment, yet until recent years it was not included in medical school training. As a result, she said, many doctors and nurses do not feel prepared or confident in caring for patients with chronic pain.

Oaklander said she often treats people who have spent years moving through the medical system without receiving a clear diagnosis. She generally separates chronic pain patients into two categories. The first includes people whose pain has an ongoing source, such as arthritis patients who feel joint pain every day. The second group, she said, is more challenging: people whose chronic pain continues even though there is no clear sign of tissue damage.

According to Oaklander, Connick belonged to that second group. X-rays can reveal broken bones, she explained, but they do not show nerve injuries. It was not until years later, when a neurologist evaluated him, that doctors recognized the nerve damage behind his symptoms and were able to treat it.

Oaklander said medication can benefit many people with pain, but it is not the only approach. If pain is tied to an orthopedic issue, for example, physical therapy may be the most appropriate treatment.

For Connick, the answer was an operation to place a peripheral nerve stimulator above his hip. The device, which is based on pacemaker technology, is implanted beneath the skin. Oaklander said it sends out harmless electrical pulses that interfere with pain messages traveling to the brain. She added that the procedure does require minor surgery and that the stimulator helps only about half of the patients who receive it.

For Connick, however, the device changed everything. “The day they implanted it and I switched it on, I had climbed seven flights of stairs before they made me stop,” he said. “Everything I hadn’t been able to do, everything that made me happy, was available to me again. I knew it instantly.”

Today, Connick has returned to his job loading trucks. He spends the entire day on his feet and says he has no pain to complain about.

Oaklander’s advice to chronic pain patients is to persist. “If you have chronic pain, don’t accept no as the final answer,” she said. She added that it is important for people living with chronic pain to hold on to purpose, optimism and hope, even when they have been treated in ways that feel demeaning.

Judy Fortin is a CNN Medical News correspondent. Linda Ciampa of Accent Health contributed to the report.

# After six years of chronic foot pain, a Massachusetts man found relief from a tiny nerve-stimulating implant

**By [Your Name]**

LYNN, Massachusetts — For six years, Timothy Connick lived with pain that followed him everywhere.

It began after a fall from a loading dock — the kind of accident that can be over in seconds but leave consequences that last for years. Connick, of Lynn, Massachusetts, developed chronic foot pain that persisted despite the kinds of treatments many patients try first: medications, rest, physical therapy and other conservative approaches.

The pain affected his ability to walk, work and move through daily life comfortably. Like many people with long-term nerve-related pain, he was left searching for an option that could help when standard treatments were not enough.

That option came at Massachusetts General Hospital, where doctors implanted a **peripheral nerve stimulator**, a device designed to interrupt pain signals before they reach the brain.

For Connick, the result was meaningful relief after years of discomfort.

## A device that targets pain at the source

Peripheral nerve stimulation, or PNS, is a treatment used for certain types of chronic pain caused by irritated or injured nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. The system typically involves placing a thin wire, called a lead, near a targeted peripheral nerve. The lead delivers mild electrical pulses that can change how pain signals are transmitted.

Rather than “curing” an underlying injury, the device is meant to reduce the intensity of pain messages traveling along the nerve.

Patients often describe the stimulation as a gentle tingling or pulsing sensation, though newer systems may work without a noticeable feeling. The device can be adjusted externally, allowing clinicians to fine-tune the stimulation based on the patient’s symptoms and response.

## Chronic foot pain can be difficult to treat

Foot pain after trauma can come from many causes, including fractures, ligament injuries, tendon damage, arthritis or nerve injury. When nerve damage is involved, the pain may feel burning, stabbing, shooting or electric. It can also persist long after the original injury has healed.

Chronic nerve pain can be especially frustrating because it may not always show up clearly on X-rays or routine imaging. Patients may look “fine” on the outside but still experience severe pain with walking, standing or even light touch.

For some patients, treatment may include anti-inflammatory medications, nerve pain medications, injections, physical therapy, orthotics or surgery. But when those treatments fail, neuromodulation — using electrical stimulation to alter nerve activity — may be considered.

## A less invasive option than some surgical procedures

Peripheral nerve stimulation is part of a broader field of pain treatment known as neuromodulation. It differs from spinal cord stimulation, which targets pain pathways near the spinal cord. PNS focuses more directly on a specific nerve in the arm, leg, head, neck or trunk.

For the right patient, that targeted approach may offer pain relief with a procedure that is less extensive than some other implanted pain devices.

Doctors typically evaluate patients carefully before recommending PNS. They may consider the location of pain, whether it follows a nerve distribution, how long symptoms have lasted, what treatments have already been tried and whether a temporary trial of stimulation improves symptoms.

## Relief after years of searching

Connick’s case highlights a growing interest in implanted and minimally invasive technologies for chronic pain — particularly as physicians seek alternatives to long-term opioid use.

Although peripheral nerve stimulators do not work for everyone, they can be life-changing for selected patients whose pain is localized and nerve-related.

For Connick, the device implanted by doctors at Massachusetts General Hospital offered what had been missing for years: a way to reduce the pain that began with one fall and became a daily burden.

Medical experts caution that anyone with chronic foot pain should be evaluated to determine the underlying cause. Treatment depends on the diagnosis, and PNS is generally considered only after other options have been tried.

But for patients like Connick, the technology can offer renewed mobility, reduced pain and a chance to return to parts of life that chronic pain had taken away.

# Chronic pain can take over a life. New nerve-stimulation treatments may offer hope for some patients

**By [Your Name]**  
**Health News Feature**

For years, 52-year-old Timothy Connick of Massachusetts tried to explain a pain that seemed to have no simple cause and no easy solution.

Some days, he says, the pain felt like burning. Other days, it was sharp, electric, or crushing — the kind of sensation that made ordinary routines difficult: walking through a grocery store, sitting through dinner, sleeping through the night.

Like many people living with chronic pain, Connick did not just struggle with symptoms. He struggled to be believed, to find the right diagnosis, and to locate treatments that did more than temporarily dull the discomfort.

“I wanted my life back,” Connick said. “But pain changes everything — your mood, your work, your relationships, even how you see yourself.”

Chronic pain is often defined as pain that lasts longer than three months or persists beyond the usual time of healing. It may follow an injury, surgery, infection, or illness. In other cases, it develops gradually or remains unexplained for years.

Health experts say chronic pain is not simply a prolonged version of acute pain. Over time, the nervous system itself can change, becoming more sensitive and more reactive. That can make pain harder to treat — and harder for patients to describe.

## A widespread and often invisible condition

The American Chronic Pain Association has long emphasized that chronic pain is a major public health problem affecting tens of millions of Americans. The organization describes chronic pain as one of the most common reasons adults seek medical care and a condition that can interfere with work, sleep, mobility, mental health and social life.

National estimates often cited by pain organizations and federal health agencies suggest that about 50 million U.S. adults live with chronic pain, with millions more experiencing “high-impact” chronic pain — pain severe enough to frequently limit daily activities.

For people like Connick, those numbers are more than statistics.

“You feel like you’re negotiating with your own body every day,” he said. “What can I do today? What will I pay for tomorrow?”

Chronic pain can arise from arthritis, spinal disorders, diabetes-related nerve damage, migraine, autoimmune disease, cancer treatment, trauma, surgery, or nerve injury. It can also occur in conditions such as complex regional pain syndrome, fibromyalgia, post-herpetic neuralgia, and small-fiber neuropathy.

## When nerves become the source of pain

Dr. Anne Louise Oaklander, a neurologist and researcher at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, has studied nerve-related pain conditions, including small-fiber neuropathy — a disorder involving damage to tiny nerve fibers that help transmit pain and temperature signals.

**Verified quote needed:** If you have a source quote from Dr. Oaklander, insert it here.  
Example placement: *“[Insert verified quote from Anne Louise Oaklander about nerve injury, small-fiber neuropathy, or chronic pain.]”*

Oaklander and other neurologists have emphasized that neuropathic pain can be especially difficult because it may occur even when routine imaging or standard tests look normal. Patients may be told nothing is wrong, even though specialized testing can sometimes reveal nerve damage.

Small-fiber neuropathy, for example, may not show up on standard nerve conduction studies, which primarily evaluate larger nerve fibers. Diagnosis may require additional tools such as a skin biopsy to measure nerve fiber density, autonomic testing, or careful clinical evaluation.

For patients, that can mean years of uncertainty.

“You start to wonder if anyone is going to figure it out,” Connick said.

## Beyond pills: a shift toward multimodal care

Treating chronic pain typically requires more than one approach. Depending on the cause, care may include physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications, nerve-pain medications, behavioral health support, sleep treatment, injections, lifestyle changes, and management of underlying disease.

Doctors increasingly describe chronic pain treatment as “multimodal,” meaning it combines medical, physical and psychological strategies.

That does not mean pain is “all in someone’s head.” Rather, chronic pain affects the brain and body together. Long-term pain can increase stress, disrupt sleep, reduce activity, and contribute to anxiety or depression — all of which can intensify pain signals.

The American Chronic Pain Association encourages patients to take an active role in pain management, including learning coping strategies, communicating clearly with clinicians, pacing activities, and seeking support.

For some patients, however, conservative treatments are not enough.

That is where neuromodulation — therapies that alter nerve activity — may enter the conversation.

## What is peripheral nerve stimulation?

Peripheral nerve stimulation, or PNS, is a treatment that uses mild electrical impulses to target specific nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves are part of the peripheral nervous system, which carries signals between the body and the central nervous system.

In a PNS procedure, a clinician places a small electrode near a targeted peripheral nerve. The electrode is connected to a pulse generator, which sends controlled electrical stimulation to the nerve. Depending on the device, the generator may be worn externally for a temporary treatment period or implanted under the skin.

The goal is not to destroy the nerve or numb the body completely. Instead, stimulation is intended to modify pain signaling.

Patients may feel a tingling sensation, though some newer systems are designed to provide stimulation that is not strongly felt. The treatment is generally considered for certain types of localized neuropathic or musculoskeletal pain, particularly when other therapies have not provided enough relief.

PNS may be used for conditions involving pain in areas such as the shoulder, knee, back, foot, or post-surgical sites, depending on the patient and the nerve involved. It is also being studied and used in selected cases for pain after amputation, trauma, or nerve injury.

## Not a cure, and not for everyone

Peripheral nerve stimulation is not appropriate for every patient with chronic pain. Doctors must first identify whether the pain pattern suggests involvement of a specific peripheral nerve or nerve region that can be targeted.

Candidates typically undergo a detailed evaluation, which may include a neurological exam, imaging, review of prior treatments, and sometimes diagnostic nerve blocks. Patients also need realistic expectations: PNS may reduce pain and improve function, but it may not eliminate pain completely.

Risks can include infection, bleeding, lead movement, discomfort at the insertion site, device malfunction, or lack of benefit. Some systems require removal after a set period, while others may involve longer-term implantation.

Still, for selected patients, clinicians say PNS can be an important option — especially at a time when the medical community continues to look for alternatives to long-term opioid therapy.

## Living with chronic pain

Connick says the hardest part has not been a single symptom, but the way chronic pain shrinks life.

He has had to plan around flare-ups, cancel commitments, and explain an illness that others cannot see. He says he has learned to measure progress differently.

“A good day isn’t necessarily a pain-free day,” he said. “Sometimes it’s just being able to do something normal.”

Pain specialists say that is often the goal: restoring function, improving sleep, reducing suffering, and helping patients reengage with life.

For many people, that requires persistence — and a care team willing to keep looking for answers.

## What patients should ask

For people living with chronic pain, experts recommend asking clinicians several key questions:

- What is the most likely cause of my pain?
- Could nerve damage or neuropathy be involved?
- Are there tests that might clarify the diagnosis?
- What treatments address the underlying cause, not just the symptoms?
- Would physical therapy, behavioral pain therapy, medications, injections, or neuromodulation be appropriate?
- Am I a candidate for peripheral nerve stimulation or another nerve-targeting treatment?
- What benefits, risks and alternatives should I consider?

Connick says he wishes he had known earlier that chronic pain is a condition worthy of serious evaluation — not a personal weakness.

“You have to keep advocating for yourself,” he said. “There may not be one magic answer, but there can be steps forward.”

counterfactuals.output:
**BOSTON (CNN Medical News)** — For years, the pain was difficult for Maria Thompson to describe — a burning ache that started in her lower back and spread down her legs, sometimes flaring without warning and sometimes lingering for weeks.

“It felt like my body was sending an alarm that nobody could turn off,” said Thompson, 47, a Boston-area school administrator. “Some days I could go to work and smile through it. Other days, I couldn’t get out of bed.”

Thompson saw primary care doctors, orthopedists, neurologists and physical therapists. Imaging showed mild spinal changes, but nothing that fully explained her symptoms. Blood tests were normal. One doctor suggested stress. Another recommended surgery. A third told her to exercise more.

Her experience is familiar to millions of Americans living with chronic pain — pain that persists for three months or longer and can outlast the injury or illness that first caused it. Experts say chronic pain is not just a symptom, but a complex condition involving the nervous system, immune system, mental health, sleep, movement, and social stressors.

## A common condition that can be hard to prove

Chronic pain affects an estimated 1 in 5 adults in the United States, according to federal health surveys, and it is among the leading causes of disability. Yet diagnosis can be frustrating because pain is deeply personal and often invisible.

“Pain is real even when the scan is normal,” said Dr. Karen Liu, a pain medicine specialist at a Boston teaching hospital. “One of the biggest challenges is that our traditional medical tools are better at finding tumors, fractures or inflammation than they are at measuring how a person’s nervous system is processing pain.”

Some chronic pain conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis, cancer-related pain or nerve damage after shingles, may have clearer biological markers. Others — including fibromyalgia, many forms of low back pain, chronic pelvic pain, migraine and complex regional pain syndrome — can be harder to confirm with a single test.

That uncertainty can leave patients feeling dismissed.

“People hear, ‘We don’t see anything,’ as ‘Nothing is wrong,’” Liu said. “Those are not the same thing.”

## The brain and body connection

Researchers increasingly describe chronic pain as a disorder of the whole pain system. In some patients, nerves remain sensitized long after an injury heals. The spinal cord and brain may become more reactive, amplifying pain signals. Stress, poor sleep, depression and anxiety can worsen pain — not because pain is “imagined,” experts say, but because the same brain networks involved in emotion and vigilance also influence pain perception.

Dr. Samuel Ortiz, a neurologist who studies pain pathways, compares chronic pain to a smoke alarm that keeps sounding after the fire is out.

“The alarm is doing what it was designed to do — protect you,” Ortiz said. “But in chronic pain, that system can become overprotective. Treatment often means calming the alarm, not just searching for a single switch to turn it off.”

For patients, the effects ripple far beyond the body. Chronic pain can disrupt work, relationships, finances and identity. People may avoid movement for fear of worsening symptoms, which can lead to muscle loss and more disability. Sleep problems can make the nervous system more sensitive, creating a cycle that is difficult to break.

## A long road to treatment

Treatment often requires trial and error. For Thompson, relief came slowly through a combination of physical therapy, nerve pain medication, cognitive behavioral therapy for pain, and changes to her work routine. She also began swimming, which allowed her to move without the impact of running.

“I kept waiting for one doctor to give me the answer,” she said. “What helped was realizing I needed a plan, not a miracle.”

That approach reflects current best practice, experts say. Rather than relying on a single medication or procedure, many pain specialists recommend a multidisciplinary model that may include:

- **Physical therapy and graded exercise** to restore mobility and reduce fear of movement  
- **Non-opioid medications**, such as anti-inflammatory drugs, acetaminophen, certain antidepressants or anti-seizure medications used for nerve pain  
- **Behavioral therapies**, including cognitive behavioral therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness and biofeedback  
- **Interventional procedures**, such as nerve blocks, steroid injections, radiofrequency ablation or spinal cord stimulation for selected patients  
- **Sleep treatment**, stress reduction and management of mood disorders  
- **Complementary therapies**, including acupuncture, massage, yoga or tai chi, when used safely alongside medical care  

The opioid crisis has reshaped pain treatment in the United States. Opioids may still be appropriate for some patients, including those with cancer pain, palliative care needs or carefully selected severe chronic pain conditions. But doctors are now more cautious because of risks that include dependence, overdose, constipation, hormonal changes and increased sensitivity to pain over time.

“The pendulum has swung hard,” said Dr. Emily Rosen, a primary care physician in Boston. “We needed to address unsafe prescribing, but we also need to make sure patients in pain are not abandoned. The goal is individualized care.”

## Barriers to care

Even when effective treatments exist, patients may struggle to access them. Multidisciplinary pain programs can be expensive, have long wait lists or lack insurance coverage. Behavioral therapy for pain may be unavailable in many communities. Physical therapy visits may be limited by insurance plans or unaffordable because of copays.

For 62-year-old James Carter, a retired transit worker from Dorchester, chronic knee and back pain forced him to leave his job earlier than planned. He tried injections, medications and physical therapy, but transportation and cost made consistent care difficult.

“Everybody told me to keep moving,” Carter said. “But when you’re choosing between a therapy copay and groceries, that’s not a real choice.”

Experts say disparities in pain treatment are well documented. Studies have found that women, older adults, people with lower incomes and patients from racial and ethnic minority groups may be less likely to have their pain taken seriously or to receive adequate treatment.

“Listening is a medical intervention,” Rosen said. “Patients do better when they feel believed and when treatment goals are realistic and shared.”

## Redefining success

For many chronic pain patients, the goal is not necessarily total elimination of pain, but better function and quality of life.

That message can be difficult to accept at first, said Dr. Liu, because patients understandably want the pain gone. But a focus on function can help people regain parts of their lives even while symptoms persist.

“We ask: Can you sleep better? Can you walk farther? Can you return to work in some capacity? Can you enjoy dinner with your family?” Liu said. “Those are meaningful outcomes.”

Thompson says she still has flares, but they no longer control her life. She has learned to pace activities, recognize early warning signs and use a set of tools — stretching, medication, heat, rest and breathing techniques — before pain spirals.

“I’m not cured,” she said. “But I’m living again.”

## Reasons for hope

New research is exploring blood-based biomarkers, brain imaging tools, genetics and wearable devices that may help doctors better classify pain and predict which treatments will work for which patients. Scientists are also studying non-opioid drugs that target specific pain pathways, as well as neuromodulation techniques that use electrical stimulation to alter nerve signaling.

Experts caution that progress will take time. Chronic pain is not one disease, and no single treatment will work for everyone. But the shift toward understanding pain as a complex, treatable condition is already changing care.

“The hopeful message is that chronic pain is not a dead end,” Ortiz said. “Even when we cannot erase pain completely, we can often reduce suffering, improve function and help people rebuild their lives.”

For patients like Thompson, that hope matters.

“You start to think your world is getting smaller and smaller,” she said. “The right care helped me open it back up.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a human-interest health journalism piece explaining chronic pain and nerve injury, centered on a man whose smashed heel caused years of agony until an implanted device using pacemaker-like technology blocked his pain signals.
counterfactuals.output:
# After a Smashed Heel, Years of Pain — and a Pacemaker for the Nerves

When the ladder slipped, the fall took only a second. The pain lasted for years.

The man — a former construction worker in his 40s — landed hard on his right foot, crushing his heel bone, the calcaneus, one of the body’s toughest but most unforgiving structures. Surgeons rebuilt what they could with metal plates and screws. The bone eventually healed. The swelling went down. The incisions closed.

But the pain did not leave.

“It felt like someone had a blowtorch on my foot,” he said. “Other times it was like stepping on glass, even when I was lying in bed.”

For many people, the end of an injury is visible: a cast comes off, an X-ray improves, a scar fades. But for patients with chronic nerve pain, recovery can be far less straightforward. The original damage may be over, yet the nervous system keeps sounding the alarm.

In his case, doctors believed the trauma from the crushed heel had injured nerves in and around the foot. What began as a mechanical injury — broken bone, torn tissue, swelling — evolved into something more complicated: chronic neuropathic pain, a condition in which damaged or overactive nerves continue to send distress signals long after the body has repaired what it can.

## When Pain Becomes Its Own Disease

Pain is supposed to protect us. Touch a hot stove and nerves in the skin send electrical messages through the spinal cord to the brain: danger. Pull away.

Acute pain is that warning system working properly. Chronic pain is different.

When pain persists for months or years, especially after a major injury, the nervous system itself can change. Nerves may become hypersensitive. The spinal cord may amplify signals. The brain may continue to interpret even light touch or ordinary movement as threatening.

“Chronic pain isn’t just pain that lasts a long time,” said one pain specialist familiar with nerve-stimulation treatments. “It can become a disease of the nervous system.”

Nerve injury can produce sensations that are hard for others to understand: burning, stabbing, buzzing, electric shocks, crushing pressure, or pain from something as mild as a bedsheet brushing the skin. The foot and ankle are especially vulnerable after severe trauma because they contain dense networks of small nerves and must bear the body’s weight with every step.

For the man with the crushed heel, walking became a calculation. A trip to the grocery store meant planning how far he could make it from the parking lot. Standing at a family gathering meant looking for a chair before he said hello. Sleep came in fragments.

Pain also narrowed his world emotionally.

“I stopped being the person I was,” he said. “You don’t want to complain every day, so you get quiet.”

## The Long Search for Relief

He tried the usual ladder of treatments: anti-inflammatory drugs, nerve-pain medications, physical therapy, injections, braces, special shoes. Some helped briefly. Others brought side effects or disappointment. Opioid painkillers dulled the worst moments but did not give him his life back, and long-term use carried its own risks.

This is a common story for people with severe chronic neuropathic pain. Treatment often requires trial and error because the source of pain is not always a single damaged structure that can be repaired. Sometimes the problem lies in the signaling.

That is where neuromodulation comes in.

Neuromodulation is a broad term for therapies that alter nerve activity, often using electrical stimulation. The technology is sometimes compared to a pacemaker, not because it treats the heart, but because it uses an implanted device to deliver carefully controlled electrical pulses inside the body.

For chronic pain, these devices do not “cure” the injury. They aim to interrupt or reshape the pain messages traveling through the nervous system.

In many patients with pain in the foot, ankle, knee or groin, doctors may consider a form of treatment called dorsal root ganglion stimulation, or DRG stimulation. The dorsal root ganglion is a small cluster of nerve cells near the spine that acts like a relay station for sensory signals from specific parts of the body. By targeting that relay, physicians can sometimes quiet pain in a very precise area, such as the heel or foot.

Other patients may receive spinal cord stimulation, which places thin wires near the spinal cord to alter pain transmission more broadly.

## A Trial Before the Implant

Before receiving a permanent implant, patients typically undergo a temporary trial. Thin leads are placed through a needle near the targeted nerves, while the pulse generator remains outside the body. For several days, the patient tests whether stimulation meaningfully reduces pain and improves function.

For him, the difference was not subtle.

“It didn’t make my foot normal,” he said. “But the screaming stopped.”

Instead of searing pain with every step, he felt pressure, soreness, and the awareness of an old injury — but no longer the same relentless electrical torment. He slept longer. He walked farther. He began to imagine errands, dinners, even short trips without fear dominating the day.

After a successful trial, surgeons implanted the permanent system. A small battery-powered pulse generator was placed under the skin, often in the lower back or buttock area, and connected to slender leads positioned near the nerve target. Using an external controller, the patient can adjust settings within limits prescribed by the care team.

The device sends mild electrical pulses that interfere with pain signaling. Some systems create a tingling sensation; newer programs may work without patients feeling the stimulation at all.

The comparison to a pacemaker is useful but imperfect. A cardiac pacemaker keeps the heart beating in rhythm. A pain stimulator changes communication in the nervous system, reducing the intensity or frequency of pain signals before they are fully perceived by the brain.

## Not a Miracle, but a Door Reopened

Doctors caution that implanted stimulators are not for everyone. Candidates are carefully evaluated, often after conservative treatments fail. Psychological screening may be included, not because pain is “in the head,” but because depression, anxiety, trauma and sleep deprivation can all influence pain and recovery. Patients must also be able to manage the device and understand that results vary.

Risks include infection, bleeding, lead movement, pain at the implant site, hardware problems and the possibility that pain relief fades over time. Some patients do not respond. Others receive partial relief rather than complete freedom from pain.

But for people who do respond, the change can be profound.

For the man with the smashed heel, the implant did not erase the accident. His foot still bears the history of the fall. He still has bad days. Cold weather can aggravate symptoms. Too much activity can bring swelling and deep aching.

But the pain no longer dictates every hour.

He can walk his dog around the block. He can stand long enough to cook. He can sit through a movie without shifting constantly. He can sleep.

In chronic pain medicine, those gains matter.

Pain specialists often measure success not only by a number on a pain scale, but by function: Can the person move more? Sleep better? Use fewer medications? Rejoin family life? Return to work or hobbies? Feel less trapped inside the body?

By those measures, the implant gave him something he had not felt in years: room to live.

## The Invisible Burden

Chronic pain affects tens of millions of people and is one of the leading causes of disability. Yet it remains poorly understood, partly because it is invisible. A person may look fine while experiencing severe nerve pain. Imaging may show a healed fracture while the nervous system continues to misfire.

That invisibility can deepen suffering. Patients often describe feeling doubted by employers, insurers, friends, even clinicians. They learn to ration their honesty.

“If you say you’re in pain every day, people don’t know what to do with that,” he said. “So you stop saying it.”

Researchers increasingly view chronic pain as a complex interaction among injured tissues, nerves, the spinal cord, the brain, immune cells, sleep, mood and life stress. That does not make the pain less real. It makes it more medically complex.

The story of one man’s crushed heel and implanted nerve stimulator reflects a larger shift in pain care: away from simply masking symptoms, and toward understanding the electrical language of pain itself.

For him, the device is always there, under the skin — a small piece of technology standing between an old injury and the life it nearly consumed.

“I know the damage is still there,” he said. “But now I can get up in the morning and think about something besides my foot. That’s a big thing.”
